meta.name: India Civ historical timeline layer (eras, polities, places, routes)
meta.source_org: Wikidata (CC0); aourednik/historical-basemaps (GPL-3.0); Wikipedia and Britannica as dating references
meta.license: Wikidata: CC0. Historical-basemaps geometry: GPL-3.0 (derived extents keep GPL-3.0). Era summaries: written by this project; sources cited per era.
meta.limitations: Historical data. Dates are rounded and negative years mean BCE (1 BCE = -1, no year 0). Extents come from a world-wide basemap with coarse, generalised borders at fixed years; they are not surveyed. Extents before 1000 CE have confidence low. Polities without a matching basemap polygon have geometry null. Routes are straight lines between documented waypoint cities, not surveyed paths. Do not merge this file with modern statistics.
meta.method: Places and capitals are chosen in pipeline/history_config.py and resolved to Wikidata QIDs from English Wikipedia titles (redirects followed) to get coordinates. Dates are curated from the cited articles. Extents: basemap features matched by NAME, unioned, clipped to lon 60-100 and lat 5-40, simplified at 0.05 degrees, rounded to 2 decimals, parts under 0.01 square degrees dropped. Routes: polylines through waypoint cities.

eras.name: Indus Valley Civilisation
eras.summary: A Bronze Age urban culture in the Indus basin and nearby regions. Its Early Harappan phase begins around 3300 BCE and its Mature phase runs from about 2600 to 1900 BCE. Sites show planned towns, standard weights and a script that scholars have not deciphered. The causes of its decline are still debated.

extent.note: No capital is known. The basemap year (2000 BCE) is after the Mature phase and shows a generalised cultural area, not a state border. Source feature NAME ['Indus valley civilization'], BORDERPRECISION [1] (source scale: 1 approximate, 3 legally defined). Clipped to lon 60-100, lat 5-40 and simplified to 0.05 degrees.

eras.name: Vedic period
eras.summary: The period in North India when the Vedic texts were composed, from about 1500 to 600 BCE. The Early Vedic phase centres on the Punjab and the Late Vedic phase on the Ganges-Yamuna region. The evidence is mostly textual, with some link to Painted Grey Ware sites. Dates and the areas of settlement are uncertain.

extent.note: The basemap draws a culture area, not a political border. The link between texts and archaeology is debated. Source feature NAME ['Vedic Aryans'], BORDERPRECISION [1] (source scale: 1 approximate, 3 legally defined). Clipped to lon 60-100, lat 5-40 and simplified to 0.05 degrees.

eras.name: Mahajanapadas
eras.summary: Sixteen large territorial states are named in early Buddhist and Jain texts for the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. Most lay in the Indo-Gangetic plain. Magadha grew to be the leading state and was ruled by the Nanda dynasty at the end of the period. The lists of states differ between texts, and many borders are unknown.

eras.name: Maurya Empire
eras.summary: An empire that Chandragupta Maurya founded in Magadha about 322 BCE. Under Ashoka, about 268 to 232 BCE, it covered most of the subcontinent except the far south. Ashoka's rock and pillar edicts are the main primary sources. The empire ended about 185 BCE.

extent.note: Basemap year 200 BCE is after the peak (about 250 BCE). Outer borders and the extent of real control are uncertain. eras.name: Post-Maurya kingdoms (Shunga, Satavahana, Kushan)
eras.summary: After the Maurya Empire ended, regional powers took its place. The Shungas ruled in the Ganges plain, the Satavahanas in the Deccan, and the Kushans in the north-west and the Gangetic plain. This was also a time of strong sea trade with the Roman world. The sources include coins, inscriptions and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea.

eras.name: Gupta Empire
eras.summary: A North Indian empire that began about 320 CE under Chandragupta I. Its power was greatest under Samudragupta and Chandragupta II in the 4th and early 5th centuries. Coins, inscriptions and the account of the Chinese monk Faxian are the main sources. The empire weakened in the late 5th century and split into regional states.

eras.name: Pallava dynasty and early Deccan kingdoms
eras.summary: The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram in the far south, and the Chalukyas of Badami ruled the Deccan. The Pandyas ruled from Madurai, and Harsha held a short-lived realm in the north. Pallava and Chalukya rulers built rock-cut and structural temples. The period ended as the Cholas and Rashtrakutas grew in power.

eras.name: Chola Empire, Chalukya and Rashtrakuta kingdoms
eras.summary: The Cholas of Thanjavur rose from about 848 CE. They reached the Ganges and sent naval raids to Southeast Asia under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I in the early 11th century. In the Deccan, the Rashtrakutas ruled about 753 to 982 and the Western Chalukyas ruled about 973 to 1189. The Cholas lost power in the 13th century to the Pandyas.

eras.name: Delhi Sultanate
eras.summary: A series of five dynasties that ruled from Delhi: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughluq, Sayyid and Lodi. The sultans expanded across North India and, for a short time, into the Deccan. The Sultanate lost most of its provinces after Timur's raid of 1398. Babur defeated the last Sultan, Ibrahim Lodi, at Panipat in 1526.

eras.name: Vijayanagara Empire and Deccan sultanates
eras.summary: The Vijayanagara Empire ruled much of South India from its capital at Vijayanagara (Hampi) after 1336. The Bahmani Sultanate formed in the Deccan in 1347 and later split into five sultanates, including Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar and Bidar. In 1565 an alliance of sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota. The empire continued in reduced form until about 1646.

eras.name: Mughal Empire
eras.summary: An empire that Babur founded after the Battle of Panipat in 1526. It reached its largest size under Aurangzeb in the late 17th and early 18th centuries. Imperial power weakened after 1707, and regional states took over. The British removed the last emperor in 1857.

eras.name: Maratha Empire
eras.summary: A state that Shivaji founded in western India and crowned himself ruler of at Raigad in 1674. After 1707 the Peshwas ruled from Pune, and a confederacy of Maratha chiefs held parts of central and north India. The Marathas lost the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. The Third Anglo-Maratha War ended the Peshwa rule in 1818.

eras.name: Sikh Empire
eras.summary: A state in the Punjab that Maharaja Ranjit Singh built from 1799, when he took Lahore. It held Punjab, Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar at its greatest size. After his death in 1839 the state became unstable. The British won the two Anglo-Sikh Wars and annexed the Punjab in 1849.

eras.name: Colonial India (East India Company and British Raj)
eras.summary: The East India Company gained control in Bengal after Plassey in 1757 and then took more land. After the revolt of 1857 the Crown took over rule in 1858, and the British Raj lasted until 1947. British India was split into provinces, which included the presidencies of Bengal, Bombay and Madras. More than 500 princely states kept internal rule under British overlordship.

eras.name: Independence and modern India (key dates)
eras.summary: The British Raj ended on 15 August 1947 with the creation of the two states of India and Pakistan. The Partition moved millions of people. India became a republic on 26 January 1950. The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew many states on the basis of language.

key_dates.event: British rule ends. The Dominions of India and Pakistan are created.
The Constitution of India takes effect and India becomes a republic.
The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 takes effect and redraws state borders.
